sections.overview: The European robin is a small, upright songbird of Europe, western Asia and parts of North Africa, where its range spans woodland, scrub and settled landscapes. It is the robin of European gardens, a member of the Old World flycatcher family, Muscicapidae. The similarly orange-breasted American robin is a different species, Turdus migratorius, in the thrush family; the shared English name reflects appearance, not close relationship. Many robins stay near their breeding range, while birds from colder northern and eastern populations move south or west for winter.
sections.identification: Adults of both sexes look alike: a bright orange-red face and breast form a bib against a grey-blue border, brown upperparts and a pale belly. At about 14 centimetres long, adults weigh roughly 14–25 grams across published reference ranges; it has a short, fine bill and long legs for its upright, quick-hopping gait. Newly fledged birds lack orange and are mottled brown with golden spots, a less conspicuous pattern that blends into leaf litter. In a partial post-juvenile moult during summer, some feathers are replaced and orange-red feathers begin to appear on the breast. The sexes remain difficult to tell apart by sight.
sections.habitat: Robins use cool, shaded places with low cover, such as deciduous woods, hedges, scrub, parks and gardens. Dense vegetation gives shelter and song perches, while patches of open soil or leaf litter make small prey accessible. Nests occupy sheltered sites, from natural cover to unusual human-made places such as flower pots. Their comfort around people is especially familiar in Britain and Ireland; elsewhere in Europe they can be more wary, so garden behaviour is not universal.
sections.diet: Most of the year, robins hunt small invertebrates such as insects and earthworms at ground level. From a low perch, one may drop onto visible prey and return to cover, or hop across litter and seize prey after a brief pause. In autumn and winter, berries and other fruits can also supplement animal food; the balance varies by season and region.
sections.behavior: Outside breeding season, a robin is usually solitary and defends feeding space from others. Both sexes can hold territories and sing during winter, when the song is often more plaintive and drawn out than the breeding song. This year-round defence helps secure familiar cover and safe feeding patches as well as food. The species is partly migratory: some populations are resident, some move only in part, and northern or eastern breeders travel to western Europe and North Africa. In Britain, local birds are joined by winter visitors from farther north and east; migration varies among populations.
sections.reproduction: The female builds a cup of moss, leaves and grass, lined with hair or plant fibres, in a cavity or other sheltered site. In Britain, four or five eggs are typical; she incubates them for about 14–16 days. The chicks are altricial, meaning they hatch helpless and need parental warmth and food. Both parents feed chicks until they fledge at about two weeks; the male may keep feeding them when the female starts a second brood. A pair often raises a second brood when conditions permit.
sections.ecology: By taking insects and other invertebrates, robins are small predators in leaf litter and low vegetation; adults can in turn be hunted by birds of prey. A Lithuanian nest-box study recorded pine martens and dormice as nest predators; other observations describe cuckoo chicks ejecting host eggs or young. In southern France, a winter study documented seasonal fruit eating and inferred that robins may contribute to seed dispersal in Mediterranean scrub. When gardeners dig, robins seize worms and grubs exposed in the soil.
sections.conservation: BirdLife International’s 2018 global assessment classified the European robin as Least Concern, reflecting its very large range and population. Global security does not mean every local population is stable. In the UK, Birds of Conservation Concern 5 (2021) places the robin on the Green List. Monitoring shows a long-term increase, interrupted by falls after severe winters and local declines in earlier atlas comparisons. Cold spells can reduce survival by making food harder to find.
